crops.notes: The rootstock sets the final size, so check it when buying; the default spacing is for a semi-dwarf tree. Most apples need a second, different variety nearby that blooms at the same time. Trees start fruiting in two to five years.
Planted as dormant crowns in a trench, which is what transplant means here. A bed crops for 15 years or more. Do not harvest in the first year, and only briefly in the second, so the roots build up.
Leaves are ready to pick a few weeks after planting out. Pinch off flower buds to keep it leafy. Blackens at the first frost and sulks below about 10 °C.
Each seed is a cluster that sends up several seedlings; thin to one. The young leaves are good to eat too.

Canes fruit in their second year, then die back; cut them out after harvest. Thornless trailing types such as Triple Crown need a trellis. Rubus fruticosus names the wider blackberry group; garden blackberries are hybrids within it.

Needs acid soil, around pH 4.5 to 5.5; most garden soil must be amended or the plants grown in raised beds of acid mix. Shallow roots like mulch and steady moisture. Two different varieties crop better than one. Values are for northern highbush; rabbiteye and southern highbush suit warmer zones.
Cut the main head while the buds are tight, before they show yellow; side shoots follow for weeks. Hot weather makes heads loose and quick to flower.
A long-season crop for a fall harvest; frost improves the flavor. Pick sprouts from the bottom of the stem up as they firm.
Compact plants that need no support and crop over a few weeks. Seed rots in cold, wet soil, so wait for it to warm.
Water evenly; heads split after a dry spell followed by heavy rain. Harvest when heads feel firm.
Sow where it will grow; carrots do not transplant. Keep the seedbed moist until seedlings appear, and thin to the in-row spacing. Grown as an annual; it flowers in its second year.
The fussiest of the cabbage family. Heat, drought, or a check in growth gives small, early heads. Fold the inner leaves over the head once it shows to keep it white.
Needs steady moisture and rich soil. Seed needs light to germinate, so press it onto the surface. Plant out after nights warm up; a long cold spell can make it bolt.
Cut leaves to a few centimetres above the soil and they regrow all season. Divide clumps every few years. The flowers are edible too.
Bolts quickly in heat, so sow small batches every few weeks in spring and again in fall. The seeds are coriander. Does not like being transplanted.
Spacing assumes plants grown up a trellis; allow about twice as much in-row space when they sprawl. Dislikes root disturbance, so start indoors in individual pots.
Sow where it will grow; it dislikes transplanting. Leaves are ready in about six weeks and seed heads later in summer. Left to flower, it self-seeds.
Needs more heat than tomatoes or peppers. Plant out only once nights stay warm; a cold spell stunts plants for weeks.

Grown from cloves planted in fall, pointed end up, and harvested the next summer when the lower leaves turn brown. Grown as an annual crop. Hardneck types such as Music suit cold winters; softneck types suit mild ones.
Grown like sweet pepper but likes it warmer; seeds sprout slowly in cool soil. Fruit grows hotter as it ripens, and dry spells at fruiting raise the heat further.
Pick the outer leaves and let the centre keep growing. Light frost sweetens the leaves, and plants often crop into winter.
Plant seedlings deep, or mound soil around the stems as they grow, to get long white shanks. Stands in the ground through frost for a late harvest.
A cool-season crop that bolts in summer heat. Sow small batches every two to three weeks; part shade helps in hot climates. Seed needs light to germinate, so cover it only lightly.
Includes cantaloupe and honeydew. Needs a long, hot season; black plastic mulch helps in cool areas. Water less as fruit ripens for sweeter melons; cantaloupes are ripe when they slip from the vine.
Spreads fast by underground runners; grow it in a container or a pot sunk in the bed. Usually planted from divisions or nursery plants, since it does not come true from seed. Tolerates part shade.
A hot-weather crop. Soak seed overnight before sowing. Pick pods small and every day or two; they toughen quickly.

Bulbs form in response to day length, so choose a type for your latitude. Short-day onions suit mild-winter regions; long-day onions suit the north. Direct sowing here means planting sets (small bulbs), 2–3 cm deep.
Flavor is strongest in lean, well-drained soil and full sun. Seed needs light to germinate, so press it onto the surface. Cut back after flowering.
Very slow to germinate; soaking seed overnight helps. Grows in part shade. It flowers and turns bitter in its second year, so most gardeners sow it fresh each year.

Use fresh seed each year; it loses vigour fast and is slow to come up. Leave roots in the ground until after a few frosts for the sweetest flavor. The sap can irritate skin in sunlight, so wear gloves when handling the leaves.
A cool-season crop sown as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it stops cropping in summer heat. Most types climb and need netting or twiggy supports.

Self-fertile, so one tree is enough. It blooms early, and a late spring frost can take the crop even where the tree itself is hardy; plant on a slope rather than in a frost pocket. Fruits on last year's wood, so prune every year to an open centre.
Needs a second variety nearby for pollination. Pick European pears mature but still firm and let them ripen indoors; tree-ripened pears turn gritty at the core. Starts fruiting in three to six years.
Climbing vines that need a pole, trellis, or teepee about 2 m tall. Slower to start than bush beans but keep cropping until frost if picked often.

Grown from seed potatoes (tubers or pieces with eyes), not seed. Mound soil over the stems as they grow so tubers stay covered and green-free. Frost kills the leaves, but the tubers underground survive a light frost.
Needs a lot of room. Count back from your first frost so fruit ripens in time; harvest when the skin is hard and the stem starts to dry.
Fast and easy. Sow a short row every week or two; roots turn woody and hot if left in the ground or grown in summer heat.

Planted as dormant canes. Summer-bearing types fruit on last year's canes; fall-bearing types such as Heritage fruit on this year's and can be cut to the ground each winter. A wire or trellis keeps rows upright. Suckers spread, so keep a mown path around the row.

Planted as crowns, with the buds just below the surface. Eat only the stalks; the leaves are poisonous. Skip harvest the first year, then pull stalks in spring and early summer. Needs a cold winter to do well.
A cool-season crop that bolts as days lengthen and warm. Sow again in late summer for a fall crop.

Planted as bare-root crowns, with the crown level with the soil. June-bearing types fruit once a year from the second season; remove their first-year flowers. Day-neutral types such as Albion fruit through summer from the first year. Replant every three or four years as yields fall.
Bush-type plants, including zucchini. Pick fruit young and often; one or two plants feed most households.

Most sweet cherries need a pollination partner; Stella is self-fertile. Net trees as fruit colours, or birds take the crop. Sour cherries (Prunus cerasus) are hardier and self-fertile, and are a separate crop.
Wind-pollinated, so plant a block of several short rows rather than one long row. Keep supersweet types apart from other corn, and give them warmer soil.
Slow to germinate and needs warm soil. Plant out once nights stay above about 13 °C; cold nights stall growth.

Grown from slips (rooted sprouts) rather than seed; indoor start here means sprouting slips from a stored root. Needs warm soil and a long season. Too much nitrogen gives leaves instead of roots. Cure the roots somewhere warm for a week or two before storing.
Leafy beet relative grown for its leaves and stems. Pick outer leaves and it keeps producing from spring into fall; it tolerates more heat than spinach.
A small woody subshrub. Needs sharp drainage and dislikes wet winters more than cold ones. Trim after flowering to keep it bushy; replace plants that turn woody after a few years.
Frost kills it. Wait until nights stay above 10 °C before planting out.
Needs heat and space; small "icebox" types such as Sugar Baby suit shorter seasons. Ripe when the spot resting on the ground turns creamy yellow and the nearest tendril dries.

Sprawling vines grown for storage. Winter squash covers several Cucurbita species; these values suit butternut types and are close for acorn and buttercup. Harvest when the rind resists a fingernail, before frost, and cure in the sun for storage.
